questions.subject: social
questions.q: On which date in 1789 did a crowd in Paris storm the Bastille?
questions.explanation: The Bastille, a fortress-prison seen as a symbol of royal tyranny, was stormed on 14 July 1789.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Before the Revolution, French society was divided into how many estates?
questions.explanation: The three estates were the clergy, the nobility and everyone else, known as the Third Estate.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Which estate included peasants, artisans, merchants and lawyers?
questions.explanation: Everyone who was not clergy or nobility belonged to the Third Estate.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Which of these was a direct tax paid to the state by members of the Third Estate in France?
questions.explanation: The taille was a direct tax paid to the state, while the tithe was paid to the Church.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Why did Louis XVI call a meeting of the Estates-General in 1789?
options: To get approval for new taxes because the treasury was short of money
questions.explanation: France's finances were in a crisis, and the King needed the Estates-General to approve new taxes.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: In the Estates-General each estate had one vote. Why did the Third Estate object to this rule?
options: It wanted the nobles to have no seats
It wanted the Church to rule France
The two privileged estates could always outvote the far larger Third Estate
It did not want any voting at all
questions.explanation: The Third Estate represented most of the population but could be outvoted two to one, so it demanded that each member vote individually.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: List three privileges enjoyed by the First and Second Estates before the Revolution.
questions.answer: Members of the first two estates were exempt from paying taxes to the state. The clergy collected the tithe from peasants, and the nobles collected feudal dues from the peasants who lived on their lands. Nobles also held the high posts in the army and government.
questions.explanation: The burden of taxes fell on the Third Estate, which created resentment.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Explain how the Constitution of 1791 limited the powers of the King.
questions.answer: The Constitution of 1791 made France a constitutional monarchy. Powers were divided among the National Assembly, which made laws, the executive and the judiciary, so the King no longer held all power himself.
keyPoints: Law-making power went to the National Assembly
Powers were separated among different institutions
questions.explanation: Power moved from one absolute ruler to elected bodies and separate institutions.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Who led the Bolshevik party in the Russian Revolution of 1917?
questions.explanation: Vladimir Lenin led the Bolsheviks, who took power in October 1917.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Who was the Tsar of Russia when the February Revolution of 1917 began?
questions.explanation: Nicholas II was forced to give up the throne after the February Revolution of 1917.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: What was a major demand of Russian peasants before 1917?
options: Transfer of the nobles' and Church land to peasants
questions.explanation: Peasants had small plots and wanted the land of nobles and the Church to be given to them.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Which idea was central to socialism?
options: Property such as land and factories should be owned collectively by society
Markets should be free of all rules
Religious leaders should govern the state
questions.explanation: Socialists criticised private ownership of property and wanted it to be controlled by society as a whole.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: How did Russia's participation in the First World War add to unrest in 1917?
options: Victories made the Tsar very popular
Heavy defeats, large casualties and food shortages weakened support for the Tsar
questions.explanation: Soldiers died in huge numbers while shortages of bread and fuel hit cities like Petrograd.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: What did the Bolshevik slogan 'Peace, Land and Bread' promise?
questions.answer: Peace meant ending Russia's part in the First World War, land meant transferring land to the peasants, and bread meant ending food shortages in the cities.
questions.explanation: The slogan matched the three main complaints of soldiers, peasants and workers.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Why was the rule of the Tsar unpopular in Russia in the early twentieth century?
questions.answer: The Tsar ruled as an autocrat and did not share real power with the Duma, which he dismissed repeatedly. Workers and peasants lived in poverty, and military defeats in war added to the anger.
questions.explanation: Political, economic and military failures combined to weaken the monarchy.

questions.subject: social
questions.topic: Nazism and the Rise of Hitler
questions.q: In which year did Adolf Hitler become Chancellor of Germany?
questions.explanation: Hitler was appointed Chancellor on 30 January 1933.

questions.subject: social
questions.topic: Nazism and the Rise of Hitler
questions.q: What was the German republic set up after the First World War called?
questions.explanation: The republic was named after the town of Weimar, where its constitution was drawn up.

questions.subject: social
questions.topic: Nazism and the Rise of Hitler
questions.q: Which treaty of 1919 imposed harsh terms on Germany after the First World War?
questions.explanation: The Treaty of Versailles took away German territory, limited its army and demanded reparations.

questions.subject: social
questions.topic: Nazism and the Rise of Hitler
questions.q: How did the Great Depression of 1929 affect Germany?
options: It caused mass unemployment and made many Germans lose faith in the Weimar government
It made Germany the richest country in Europe
It had no effect on Germany
questions.explanation: Economic hardship pushed many voters towards extreme parties such as the Nazis.

questions.subject: social
questions.topic: Nazism and the Rise of Hitler
questions.q: What did the Enabling Act of March 1933 do?
options: Allowed Hitler to make laws without the approval of the Reichstag
questions.explanation: It gave Hitler's government the power to rule by decree and ended parliamentary democracy.

questions.subject: social
questions.topic: Nazism and the Rise of Hitler
questions.q: Name any three groups of people persecuted by the Nazi regime.
questions.answer: The Nazis persecuted Jews, Roma and Sinti, people with disabilities, and political opponents such as communists.
questions.explanation: Millions were imprisoned or killed under Nazi rule.

questions.subject: social
questions.topic: Nazism and the Rise of Hitler
questions.q: Explain how the Treaty of Versailles helped Hitler to gain support.
questions.answer: Many Germans felt humiliated by the war guilt clause, heavy reparations, loss of territory and limits on the army. Hitler promised to undo the treaty and restore German pride, which attracted support.
questions.explanation: Resentment against the treaty was used for nationalist propaganda.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Which line of latitude passes almost through the middle of India?
questions.explanation: The Tropic of Cancer (23.5 degrees N) divides India into almost two equal parts.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Which is the southernmost point of the Indian Union?
questions.explanation: Indira Point, on Great Nicobar Island, is the southernmost point of India.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Which city lies close to the Standard Meridian of India at 82 degrees 30 minutes E?
questions.explanation: The Standard Meridian passes near Mirzapur in Uttar Pradesh, and Indian Standard Time is based on it.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: About what is the difference in local time between the easternmost and westernmost parts of India?
questions.explanation: India extends about 29 degrees in longitude, and each degree equals four minutes, giving nearly two hours.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Which is the oldest fold mountain range in India?
questions.explanation: The Aravali range is among the oldest fold mountains, while the Himalayas are young.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Why are the northern plains of India so fertile?
options: They were formed by alluvium deposited by the Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra rivers
They were formed from volcanic lava
They are made of coral limestone
They are covered by sand blown from the Thar
questions.explanation: Rivers have laid down rich silt over millions of years, giving fertile alluvial soil.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Name the three parallel ranges of the Himalayas from north to south.
questions.answer: From north to south the ranges are the Himadri (Greater Himalaya), the Himachal (Lesser Himalaya) and the Shiwaliks.
questions.explanation: The Himadri is the highest and the Shiwaliks the lowest.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: How did the opening of the Suez Canal in 1869 increase the importance of India's location?
questions.answer: The canal shortened the sea route between Europe and Asia. India's central position on the Indian Ocean gave it easy access to West Asia, Africa and Europe on one side and South-East and East Asia on the other.
keyPoints: Shorter sea route between Europe and Asia
India lies in the centre of the Indian Ocean routes
Easy access to both east and west
questions.explanation: India's location makes it a natural link for trade.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Which peninsular river is known as the Dakshin Ganga?
questions.explanation: The Godavari is the longest peninsular river and is called Dakshin Ganga.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: The Ganga is formed at Devprayag by the meeting of the Alaknanda and which other stream?
questions.explanation: The Bhagirathi, which rises from the Gangotri glacier, joins the Alaknanda at Devprayag.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: What is the Brahmaputra called in Tibet?
questions.explanation: The Brahmaputra rises in Tibet, where it is known as the Tsangpo.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Which pair of rivers flows west into the Arabian Sea through rift valleys?
questions.explanation: The Narmada and Tapi are the main west-flowing peninsular rivers and form estuaries.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Why do Himalayan rivers carry water throughout the year while many peninsular rivers dry up in summer?
options: Himalayan rivers get water from melting snow as well as rain, while peninsular rivers depend mainly on rain
Peninsular rivers have no rainfall at all
Himalayan rivers flow only in winter
questions.explanation: Snow and glaciers feed Himalayan rivers even in dry months, making them perennial.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: What is a delta? Name one delta in India.
questions.answer: A delta is a triangular area of land formed at the mouth of a river where it deposits the silt it has carried. The Ganga-Brahmaputra delta, which includes the Sundarbans, is an example.
keyPoints: Formed at the river mouth by deposited silt
questions.explanation: Deltas are very fertile because of the deposited sediment.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Give three reasons why rivers are important to the economy of a country.
questions.answer: Rivers provide water for irrigation and drinking, can be used to generate hydroelectricity, serve as waterways for transport, and deposit fertile soil along their banks.
questions.explanation: Many early civilisations grew along rivers for these reasons.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Which type of climate does India have?
questions.explanation: India's climate is described as tropical monsoon because rainfall depends on the seasonal monsoon winds.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: From which direction do the winds that bring summer rainfall to India blow?
questions.explanation: The south-west monsoon blows from the sea towards land from June to September.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Which season in India lasts roughly from December to February?
questions.explanation: The cold weather season, or winter, lasts from about December to February.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Which place in Meghalaya is famous for very heavy rainfall?
questions.explanation: Mawsynram, near Cherrapunji, lies on the windward side of the Khasi hills and gets extremely heavy rain.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: What brings winter rainfall to north-western India, which is useful for the wheat crop?
questions.explanation: Western disturbances are weather systems from the Mediterranean region that bring winter showers.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Why does the western slope of the Western Ghats get far more rain than the Deccan Plateau just east of it?
options: It is farther from the sea
The Deccan lies in the rain shadow, since moist winds drop most rain on the windward slope
The Western Ghats are lower than the Deccan
Rain falls only in winter on the western slope
questions.explanation: Moist winds rise over the Ghats, cool and give heavy rain, leaving the leeward side dry.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Name the four seasons of India.
questions.answer: The four seasons are the cold weather season, the hot weather season, the south-west monsoon season and the season of the retreating monsoon.
questions.explanation: These seasons follow the pattern of monsoon winds and temperature.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Why is the monsoon described as a unifying bond for India?
questions.answer: The monsoon decides when crops are sown and harvested across the country and influences festivals and the rhythm of life. Because most of India depends on it for water and farming, it links the economy and culture of different regions.
questions.explanation: The shared dependence on the monsoon creates a common pattern across diverse regions.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Teak and sal are common in which type of forest?
questions.explanation: Teak and sal are the main trees of the tropical deciduous or monsoon forests.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: In which state are the Gir forests, home to the Asiatic lion?
questions.explanation: The Gir National Park in Gujarat is the natural home of the Asiatic lion.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Mangrove forests, such as those of the Sundarbans, grow in
options: Salty tidal water of deltas and coasts
questions.explanation: Mangrove trees have special roots that survive in salty, waterlogged tidal areas.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Which animal is the Kaziranga National Park in Assam especially known for?
questions.explanation: Kaziranga is famous for its population of the one-horned rhinoceros.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Why are thorny bushes and cacti common in the dry regions of Rajasthan?
options: The area gets very heavy rain
The region is covered with snow
Thorns, thick stems and deep roots help plants lose less water in low rainfall
questions.explanation: Such plants are adapted to survive in areas with little rainfall.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Name any two measures taken in India to protect wildlife.
questions.answer: India has created national parks, wildlife sanctuaries and biosphere reserves, started projects such as Project Tiger in 1973, and passed the Wildlife Protection Act of 1972.
questions.explanation: Legal protection and protected areas help save endangered species.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Explain why India has a rich variety of plants and animals.
questions.answer: India has varied relief, soils and climates, from rainy forests and wet coasts to deserts and snowy mountains. These different conditions allow many different kinds of plants and animals to live in the country.
questions.explanation: Diversity of habitats leads to diversity of life.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: How often is the Census of India conducted?
questions.explanation: The Census counts the population once every ten years.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: What does the term sex ratio mean?
questions.explanation: In India the sex ratio is expressed as the number of females per 1000 males.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Which Indian state has the largest population?
questions.explanation: Uttar Pradesh has been the most populous state in all recent censuses.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Which condition helps make the northern plains densely populated?
options: Fertile soil, flat land and plentiful water
questions.explanation: Flat fertile land with water supports farming and large settlements.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: What happens if the death rate falls sharply while the birth rate stays high?
options: The number of children goes down
questions.explanation: Population growth is the difference between the birth rate and the death rate, so a larger gap means faster growth.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Define migration. Give one push factor and one pull factor.
questions.answer: Migration is the movement of people from one place to another to live or work. Lack of jobs is a push factor, while better employment and facilities in cities are pull factors.
keyPoints: Movement from one place to another
Pull factor: better jobs or facilities
questions.explanation: Push factors drive people away from a place, and pull factors attract them to another.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: How does the age composition of a population affect a country's economy?
questions.answer: A large working-age group can raise production and incomes, while many children and old people depend on workers and need spending on schools and care. The balance between workers and dependents shapes the economy.
keyPoints: Working-age group produces goods and services
questions.explanation: The share of workers decides how many people each worker supports.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: The word democracy comes from the Greek words demos and kratia. What do they mean?
questions.explanation: Demos means people and kratia means rule, so democracy is rule by the people.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: In a democracy, who ultimately holds power?
questions.explanation: In a democracy people choose their rulers and hold them responsible.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Which of the following is an essential feature of democracy?
options: Free and fair elections in which all adults can vote
A ban on all opposition parties
questions.explanation: Regular free and fair elections are the basic test of a democracy.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: How did General Pinochet come to power in Chile in 1973?
options: By overthrowing the elected government of Salvador Allende in a military coup
By a vote of the United Nations
questions.explanation: A military coup removed the elected government, and Chile was ruled by a dictatorship until 1990.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: What does the principle of one person, one vote, one value mean?
options: Each voter may vote only once in a lifetime
Every adult's vote counts equally, whatever their wealth or background
questions.explanation: Political equality means each citizen's vote carries the same weight.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Why is a country that holds elections but bans all opposition parties not a true democracy?
options: Because voters have no real choice between competing parties
Because it has too many voters
Because elections are held too often
questions.explanation: Without real choice and open competition, elections cannot make rulers accountable.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: State any two arguments in favour of democracy.
questions.answer: Democracy makes the government accountable to citizens, improves the quality of decisions through discussion, gives dignity and equality to citizens, and allows mistakes to be corrected.
questions.explanation: Democracy gives people a say in how they are governed.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Why is a democratic government considered more accountable than a dictatorship?
questions.answer: In a democracy rulers must face regular elections and can be removed by voters, and they must follow rules and answer to people and institutions. A dictator does not face such checks.
questions.explanation: Accountability depends on the ability of citizens to choose and remove rulers.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Who was the Chairman of the Drafting Committee of the Indian Constituent Assembly?
questions.explanation: Dr B. R. Ambedkar chaired the Drafting Committee, while Dr Rajendra Prasad presided over the Assembly.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: On which date did the Constitution of India come into effect?
questions.explanation: It was adopted on 26 November 1949 and came into force on 26 January 1950, celebrated as Republic Day.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: What was the system of racial discrimination followed in South Africa until the 1990s called?
questions.explanation: Under apartheid people were classified by race and denied equal rights.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Who became president of South Africa after the first multiracial elections of 1994?
questions.explanation: Nelson Mandela, who had spent years in prison for opposing apartheid, became president in 1994.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Why does a country need a constitution?
options: To make citizens pay more tax
To set the rules for forming the government and limit its powers
questions.explanation: A constitution creates trust between citizens, decides who has power and protects against misuse of power.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: What is the Preamble of the Constitution? State any two ideals it mentions.
questions.answer: The Preamble is the introductory statement of the Constitution that sets out its basic values and aims. It mentions ideals such as justice, liberty, equality and fraternity.
questions.explanation: The Preamble reflects the philosophy of the Constitution.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Describe the role of the Constituent Assembly in making the Constitution of India.
questions.answer: The Constituent Assembly, elected in 1946, met for about three years, held long debates on each provision, and drafted the Constitution, which it adopted in November 1949. Its members represented different regions and opinions.
keyPoints: Debated provisions for about three years
questions.explanation: The Assembly's discussions produced a document accepted widely by the country.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: What is the minimum age at which a citizen can vote in India?
questions.explanation: The voting age in India is 18 years.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: What is the list of all persons eligible to vote in an area called?
questions.explanation: The electoral roll, or voters' list, is prepared before elections.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Which independent body is responsible for conducting elections in India?
questions.explanation: The Election Commission supervises and conducts elections to Parliament and State Assemblies.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Who appoints the Prime Minister of India?
options: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha
The Chairman of the Rajya Sabha
questions.explanation: The President appoints the leader of the party or coalition that has majority support in the Lok Sabha.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Which of these together make up the Parliament of India?
options: The President, Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha
The Supreme Court and High Courts
questions.explanation: Parliament consists of the President and the two Houses.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Why is a Model Code of Conduct applied to parties during elections?
options: To keep the contest fair by preventing misuse of government power by the ruling party
questions.explanation: The code ensures a level playing field between ruling and opposition parties.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Distinguish between the legislature and the executive.
questions.answer: The legislature, such as Parliament, makes laws and controls the government, while the executive, such as the Prime Minister, Council of Ministers and civil servants, carries out and enforces those laws.
questions.explanation: Each organ has a different function in government.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Why is an independent judiciary important in a democracy?
questions.answer: An independent judiciary can protect citizens' rights, settle disputes fairly and check whether laws and actions of the government follow the Constitution, without pressure from the government.
keyPoints: Checks the government under the Constitution
questions.explanation: Without independence, courts could not act as a check on power.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: How many Fundamental Rights does the Indian Constitution guarantee?
questions.explanation: The six Fundamental Rights are equality, freedom, against exploitation, freedom of religion, cultural and educational rights, and constitutional remedies.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Which Fundamental Right lets citizens approach the courts if their rights are violated?
questions.explanation: Dr Ambedkar called this right the heart and soul of the Constitution.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Under which right is untouchability abolished?
questions.explanation: The Right to Equality prohibits discrimination and abolishes untouchability.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: A factory owner makes a twelve-year-old child work in a dangerous mine. Which right is violated?
questions.explanation: The Right against Exploitation prohibits forced labour and the employment of children below fourteen in hazardous work.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: A state bans a community from running schools that teach in its own language. Which right is mainly violated?
questions.explanation: Minorities have the right to conserve their language and culture and to set up their own educational institutions.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Name any three writs that courts can issue to protect Fundamental Rights.
questions.answer: Courts can issue writs such as habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari and quo warranto.
questions.explanation: Writs are orders by the Supreme Court or High Courts to enforce rights.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Why are reasonable restrictions placed on rights such as freedom of speech? Give an example.
questions.answer: Rights of one person must not harm the rights and safety of others or the public order. For example, freedom of speech does not allow someone to spread false and harmful statements or incite violence.
questions.explanation: Freedom is balanced with responsibility.

questions.subject: social
questions.topic: Village Economy and People as Resource
questions.q: Which of these is an example of physical capital?
questions.explanation: Physical capital includes tools, machines and buildings used in production.

questions.subject: social
questions.topic: Village Economy and People as Resource
questions.q: Growing more than one crop on the same piece of land in a year is called
questions.explanation: Multiple cropping is the most common way to increase production from a given land.

questions.subject: social
questions.topic: Village Economy and People as Resource
questions.q: Which input was an important part of the Green Revolution in India?
questions.explanation: HYV seeds, along with fertilisers and irrigation, raised wheat and rice yields.

questions.subject: social
questions.topic: Village Economy and People as Resource
questions.q: Farming and fishing belong to which sector of the economy?
questions.explanation: Activities that use natural resources directly, such as agriculture, are in the primary sector.

questions.subject: social
questions.topic: Village Economy and People as Resource
questions.q: Why is spending on education and health called investment in human capital?
options: It improves people's skills and productivity, which raises their income and the country's output
It increases the amount of land
It reduces the number of workers
questions.explanation: Healthy and educated people work more productively and earn more.

questions.subject: social
questions.topic: Village Economy and People as Resource
questions.q: Why cannot a village simply raise farm output by cultivating more land?
options: The area of cultivable land is fixed, so output must rise through multiple cropping or modern methods
Land cannot be used for farming
questions.explanation: Since the land area is largely fixed, farmers must use the same land more intensively.

questions.subject: social
questions.topic: Village Economy and People as Resource
questions.q: Name the four factors of production.
questions.answer: The four factors of production are land, labour, physical capital and human capital (knowledge and enterprise).
questions.explanation: All production needs a combination of these factors.

crossCheck.note: Standard CBSE/NCERT factors are land, labour, physical capital and entrepreneurship. The proposed answer puts human capital in place of entrepreneurship and then describes it as enterprise, which mixes two factors. Check against the textbook wording. Reviewed: the answer follows the NCERT Class 9 Economics wording (human capital = knowledge and enterprise); kept.

questions.subject: social
questions.topic: Village Economy and People as Resource
questions.q: Explain how education can raise both a person's income and the country's growth.
questions.answer: Education gives people skills and knowledge so that they can do better-paid and more productive work. As many such workers raise output and invent new methods, the whole economy grows.
questions.explanation: People with more skills create more value.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Which scheme, begun in 2005, guarantees 100 days of wage employment to rural households?
questions.explanation: The National Rural Employment Guarantee Act promises up to 100 days of work a year to rural households that ask for it.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: The Public Distribution System in India supplies
options: Food grains at subsidised prices through ration shops
questions.explanation: Ration shops sell items such as rice, wheat and sugar at lower prices.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: What is the main role of the Food Corporation of India?
options: Buying food grains from farmers and keeping buffer stocks
questions.explanation: The FCI buys grain at minimum support prices and stores it for distribution.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: In which region of British India did a severe famine occur in 1943?
questions.explanation: The Bengal famine of 1943 killed millions and shaped India's later focus on food security.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Why can food insecurity exist even when the country has enough grain?
options: Poor families may lack the money to buy it, so access matters as well as supply
questions.explanation: Food security needs availability, accessibility and affordability.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: What is the poverty line?
questions.answer: The poverty line is a minimum level of income or spending needed to buy basic necessities such as food, clothing and shelter. People below it are considered poor.
keyPoints: Minimum level of income or spending
Based on basic needs such as food
Those below it are called poor
questions.explanation: It is a way of measuring poverty.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Explain any two causes of poverty in India.
questions.answer: Large numbers of people lack steady employment or land and depend on low-paid work. Low levels of education and health, and unequal distribution of income and assets, also keep families poor.
questions.explanation: Poverty arises from lack of income-earning opportunities and unequal resources.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: In which year was the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen adopted in France?
questions.explanation: The National Assembly adopted the Declaration in August 1789.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Which king of France was executed by guillotine in January 1793?
questions.explanation: Louis XVI was tried for treason and executed in January 1793 after the monarchy was abolished.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Under the Constitution of 1791, who were called active citizens?
options: Men above 25 who paid taxes equal to at least three days' wages of a labourer
questions.explanation: Only active citizens could vote, while men and women with less property were passive citizens.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: In which year was France declared a republic?
questions.explanation: After the monarchy was abolished, France became a republic in 1792.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Why did the system of active and passive citizens go against the spirit of the Declaration of Rights?
options: It made the nobles equal to peasants
The Declaration spoke of equal rights, but property conditions kept poorer men from voting
questions.explanation: The Declaration said men were born free and equal, yet voting was restricted by wealth.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: State any three rights mentioned in the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen.
questions.answer: The Declaration stated that men have natural rights such as liberty, property, security and resistance to oppression. It also declared equality before the law and freedom of speech and opinion.
questions.explanation: These rights were described as natural and belonging to every man.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Why did the National Assembly abolish feudal obligations in August 1789?
questions.answer: Peasants had risen against their lords in many parts of France, and the Assembly wanted to calm the countryside. It abolished feudal obligations and the tithe, which removed many privileges of nobles and the Church.
keyPoints: Privileges of nobles and clergy reduced
questions.explanation: The decision responded to rural unrest and the demand for equality.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: What was the Russian city of Petrograd called earlier?
questions.explanation: St Petersburg was renamed Petrograd in 1914, early in the First World War.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Which famous work was published in 1848 by Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels?
questions.explanation: The Communist Manifesto set out their ideas on class struggle and socialism.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: What was the Duma in Russia?
options: An elected parliament set up after the 1905 revolution
questions.explanation: The Tsar allowed an elected Duma but often dismissed it when it opposed him.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: What happened on Bloody Sunday in 1905?
options: A coup brought Lenin to power
Peaceful workers marching to the Winter Palace were fired upon by troops
The Tsar gave up his throne
questions.explanation: The massacre of the marchers set off the revolution of 1905.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: In which year was the Soviet Union (USSR) formed?
questions.explanation: The USSR was formally created in 1922 after the civil war.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Why did the Bolsheviks agree to the harsh Treaty of Brest-Litovsk with Germany in 1918?
options: They wanted to end the war, as promised, and keep their hold on power at home
They wished to give Russia to Germany
They had been defeated in a civil war
questions.explanation: Lenin had promised peace, and the new government needed to focus on staying in power.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: What were the Five Year Plans in the Soviet Union?
questions.answer: They were plans, begun in 1928, in which the government fixed targets for industry and agriculture and directed the economy. They aimed at rapid industrial growth under state control.
questions.explanation: The Soviet economy was run through central planning.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Why did the February Revolution of 1917 begin in Petrograd?
questions.answer: Petrograd faced severe shortages of bread and fuel, and women workers and factory workers marched and struck. Soldiers sent to control them joined the protesters, and the Tsar lost control.
questions.explanation: The capital's hardships and the army's support for the crowds toppled the Tsar.

questions.subject: social
questions.topic: Nazism and the Rise of Hitler
questions.q: Which symbol was used by the Nazi party?
questions.explanation: The Nazis used the swastika as their emblem on flags and badges.

questions.subject: social
questions.topic: Nazism and the Rise of Hitler
questions.q: In which book, written in prison, did Hitler set out his ideas?
questions.explanation: Mein Kampf, meaning My Struggle, was written by Hitler after the failed Munich uprising of 1923.

questions.subject: social
questions.topic: Nazism and the Rise of Hitler
questions.q: What did the Nazi idea of Lebensraum mean?
options: Living space for Germans through taking over other territories
questions.explanation: Hitler argued Germany needed more land, which was used to justify expansion and war.

questions.subject: social
questions.topic: Nazism and the Rise of Hitler
questions.q: Which event began the Second World War in Europe in 1939?
questions.explanation: Britain and France declared war on Germany after its invasion of Poland in September 1939.

questions.subject: social
questions.topic: Nazism and the Rise of Hitler
questions.q: How did the Nazis use propaganda to win mass support?
options: They used posters, films, radio and rallies to spread nationalist messages and blame minorities
questions.explanation: Under Goebbels, mass media were used to promote the Nazi message and to shape public opinion.

questions.subject: social
questions.topic: Nazism and the Rise of Hitler
questions.q: What was the Holocaust?
questions.answer: The Holocaust was the systematic persecution and mass murder of about six million Jews, along with other groups, by the Nazi regime in Europe during the Second World War.
questions.explanation: It involved ghettos, camps and mass killing.

questions.subject: social
questions.topic: Nazism and the Rise of Hitler
questions.q: How did the Nazis try to shape young people through the Hitler Youth?
questions.answer: The Nazis made children join youth organisations that taught loyalty to Hitler, hatred of those labelled enemies and physical and military training. Schools also taught Nazi ideas.
keyPoints: Youth groups taught loyalty to Hitler
questions.explanation: Control of the young was meant to secure long-term support for the regime.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: The Western Ghats run parallel to which water body?
questions.explanation: The Western Ghats lie along the western coast of the peninsula, close to the Arabian Sea.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Which desert lies in the western part of India?
questions.explanation: The Thar Desert covers parts of Rajasthan and neighbouring areas.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: The Lakshadweep Islands are mainly made of
questions.explanation: Lakshadweep consists of coral islands and atolls in the Arabian Sea.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: What is the newer, fertile alluvium deposited by rivers in floodplains called?
questions.explanation: Khadar is newer alluvium, while Bhangar is older alluvium found on higher ground.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Why are the Himalayas called young fold mountains?
options: They are made of volcanic ash
They formed recently by folding and are still rising, with high peaks and deep valleys
questions.explanation: They were formed by the collision of plates and are geologically young.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Name the two island groups that belong to India and the seas in which they lie.
questions.answer: The Andaman and Nicobar Islands lie in the Bay of Bengal, and the Lakshadweep Islands lie in the Arabian Sea.
keyPoints: Andaman and Nicobar in the Bay of Bengal
questions.explanation: These are India's two main island groups.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Describe two ways in which the Himalayas influence India.
questions.answer: The Himalayas block cold winds from Central Asia and trap monsoon winds to bring rain. They are also the source of perennial rivers such as the Ganga and Brahmaputra.
questions.explanation: The range shapes climate and water supply in northern India.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Which river forms the Dhuandhar Falls near Jabalpur?
questions.explanation: The Narmada plunges over the Dhuandhar Falls in Madhya Pradesh.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: From which glacier does the Yamuna rise?
questions.explanation: The Yamuna rises from the Yamunotri glacier in Uttarakhand and joins the Ganga at Prayagraj.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Which of these is a salt water lake in Rajasthan?
questions.explanation: Sambhar Lake in Rajasthan is known for its salt water and salt production.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Where does the Indus river rise?
questions.explanation: The Indus rises in Tibet near Mansarovar and flows through Ladakh before entering Pakistan.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Which river is called the Sorrow of Bihar because of its floods?
questions.explanation: The Kosi often changes its course and causes heavy floods in Bihar.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Why are floods common in the Ganga-Brahmaputra plains in the monsoon?
options: There is no rain in the monsoon
Heavy monsoon rain adds huge amounts of water to rivers that flow slowly across flat land
questions.explanation: Large volumes of water and a gentle slope make the rivers overflow.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: What is a river basin?
questions.answer: A river basin is the entire area drained by a river and its tributaries. It is separated from neighbouring basins by a high ground called a watershed.
keyPoints: Area drained by a river and its tributaries
Separated from others by a watershed
questions.explanation: Rivers collect water from their whole basin.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Name two causes of river pollution and suggest two measures to reduce it.
questions.answer: Rivers are polluted by untreated sewage and industrial waste and by solid waste dumped in them. Pollution can be reduced by treating sewage and factory waste before releasing it and by stopping dumping in rivers.
questions.explanation: Cleaner rivers need both rules and treatment plants.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: What is the loo?
options: A cold wind of the Himalayas
A hot, dry wind blowing over the northern plains in summer
A cyclone in the Bay of Bengal
questions.explanation: The loo blows in May and June over northern and north-western India.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Hill stations are cooler than the plains because temperature falls as we go higher. Which factor is this?
questions.explanation: Temperature drops with increasing height above sea level.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Which coastal region receives much of its rainfall in October and November from the retreating monsoon?
questions.explanation: The retreating monsoon picks up moisture from the Bay of Bengal and rains on the Tamil Nadu coast.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Which pre-monsoon showers help the ripening of mangoes in Kerala and Karnataka?
questions.explanation: Mango showers fall at the end of summer in the south.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Why do coastal cities such as Mumbai have a smaller temperature range than inland cities such as Delhi?
options: Mumbai is at a higher altitude
Delhi is next to the sea
The sea moderates temperatures near the coast, while inland places have extreme climates
questions.explanation: Water heats and cools slowly, so coasts have milder weather.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: What is meant by the term monsoon?
questions.answer: The monsoon is a system of winds that reverses direction with the seasons. In summer winds blow from the sea to the land bringing rain, and in winter they blow from land to sea.
keyPoints: Summer winds bring rain from the sea
questions.explanation: The word monsoon comes from an Arabic word for season.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Why does Rajasthan have a larger range of temperature than Kerala?
questions.answer: Rajasthan lies inland, far from the sea, with dry air and sandy soil that heat up quickly by day and cool quickly at night. Kerala is near the sea, whose moist air moderates temperature.
keyPoints: Rajasthan is far from the sea and dry
Sandy desert heats and cools fast
Kerala is moderated by the sea
questions.explanation: Distance from the sea strongly affects temperature range.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Which tree is common in the coniferous forests of the Himalayas?
questions.explanation: Deodar, pine, fir and spruce grow in the cooler mountain forests.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Which big cat is found in the Sundarbans?
questions.explanation: The Sundarbans in the Ganga delta are famous for the Royal Bengal tiger.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Forests that grow in regions with more than 200 cm of rainfall are mostly
questions.explanation: Heavy rain throughout the year supports dense, evergreen vegetation.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: In which year was Project Tiger launched in India?
questions.explanation: Project Tiger began in 1973 to protect the tiger and its habitat.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Which of these trees is typical of tropical evergreen forests?
questions.explanation: Mahogany, ebony and rosewood grow in heavy-rainfall evergreen forests.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Why does the destruction of forests lead to loss of animal species?
options: Forests are the homes of animals, giving food and shelter, which are lost when forests are cleared
Forests are not connected to animals
questions.explanation: Habitat loss is a major reason why species decline.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: What is a biosphere reserve? Give one example.
questions.answer: A biosphere reserve is a large protected area where plants, animals and local ways of living are conserved together. The Sundarbans and the Nilgiri region are examples.
keyPoints: Conserves plants, animals and local life
Example such as Sundarbans or Nilgiri
questions.explanation: Biosphere reserves protect whole ecosystems.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Explain how mangrove forests protect coastal areas.
questions.answer: The roots of mangroves hold the soil and reduce erosion, and the trees break the force of waves and storms. They also provide breeding places for fish and other creatures.
keyPoints: Roots hold soil and reduce erosion
Reduce force of waves and storms
questions.explanation: Mangroves act as natural barriers along the coast.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: In the Indian census, which age group is usually treated as the working-age group?
questions.explanation: People aged 15 to 59 are mainly the productive workers of a population.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: The number of persons living per square kilometre is called
questions.explanation: Density is calculated by dividing the population by the area.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: In which year was the first synchronous census of India held?
questions.explanation: The first synchronous census, counting all areas at the same time, was held in 1881.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Which age group is classed as adolescents in India's population policy?
questions.explanation: Adolescents form an important section that needs care in health and education.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: What is a major cause of migration from villages to cities?
options: A search for jobs and better services
questions.explanation: Many people move to cities for work, education and health care.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Why can a large share of young people be both an opportunity and a challenge for a country?
options: A big young workforce can drive growth, but it needs education, health and jobs
questions.explanation: The benefit depends on how well the country trains and employs its young.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Define birth rate and death rate.
questions.answer: The birth rate is the number of live births per thousand people in a year, and the death rate is the number of deaths per thousand people in a year.
keyPoints: Birth rate: births per 1000 per year
Death rate: deaths per 1000 per year
questions.explanation: The difference between the two gives the natural increase.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Explain two ways in which a fast-growing population can put pressure on resources.
questions.answer: A larger population needs more food, water, housing and energy, so these resources may become scarce. It also needs more schools, hospitals and jobs, which governments may find hard to provide quickly.
keyPoints: More demand for food, water and housing
More need for schools and hospitals
questions.explanation: Growth in numbers can outpace growth in facilities.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Which of the following is a non-democratic form of government?
questions.explanation: A military dictatorship is ruled by the army without the consent of the people.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Who described democracy as government of the people, by the people and for the people?
questions.explanation: Abraham Lincoln, a former American president, gave this well-known definition.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: What does universal adult franchise mean?
options: Every adult citizen has the right to vote
questions.explanation: In a democracy all adults have a vote, whatever their wealth, sex or background.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Which of these is a democratic practice?
options: Banning newspapers that criticise the government
A citizen's right to criticise government policy without fear of punishment
questions.explanation: Freedom to express opinion is a basic part of democracy.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Why is it said that democracy helps to settle conflicts peacefully?
options: Elections and discussion give different groups a way to settle differences without violence
It gives all power to one group
questions.explanation: Democratic processes allow groups to negotiate and accept results of fair votes.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: What is a representative democracy?
questions.answer: In a representative democracy citizens elect representatives who take decisions and make laws on their behalf, instead of everyone deciding directly. It is used in large countries such as India.
keyPoints: Used because direct decisions by all are not practical in large countries
questions.explanation: Most modern democracies are representative.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Why is it not enough for a democracy to hold elections? Mention two other conditions.
questions.answer: Elections alone do not make a democracy if citizens lack rights or if rulers misuse power. A democracy also needs guaranteed rights such as freedom of speech and independent institutions such as courts, with rule of law.
keyPoints: Independent courts and rule of law
questions.explanation: Democracy needs limits on power as well as voting.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Who was the President of the Constituent Assembly of India?
questions.explanation: Dr Rajendra Prasad presided over the Assembly and later became the first President of India.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: What does the word sovereign in the Preamble mean?
options: The country is ruled by a foreign power
The country can be changed by anyone
The country takes its own decisions without outside control
questions.explanation: A sovereign state has the supreme right to decide its own internal and external affairs.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: What does secular mean in the Indian Constitution?
options: The state has no official religion and treats all religions equally
Only one community can hold office
questions.explanation: A secular state does not favour or discriminate against any religion.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Who moved the Objectives Resolution in the Constituent Assembly in December 1946?
questions.explanation: Nehru's Objectives Resolution laid down the aims that guided the framing of the Constitution.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Why do leaders prefer a written constitution with basic rules that cannot be changed easily?
options: It gives lasting basic rules that no government can alter at will
It lets each ruler change it daily
It removes the need for laws
It has no effect on government
questions.explanation: Stable basic rules protect citizens and prevent misuse of power.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: After apartheid, South African leaders chose cooperation and reconciliation rather than revenge. What does this show?
options: They gave up the idea of a constitution
Leaders were willing to compromise to build a democracy that included all groups
questions.explanation: Negotiation between former rivals helped the country move to a shared democratic constitution.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: What does the word republic mean in the Preamble?
questions.answer: A republic is a country in which the head of state is elected and does not hold office by heredity. In India the President is elected for a fixed term.
keyPoints: India's President serves a fixed term
questions.explanation: A republic is the opposite of a hereditary monarchy.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Why do constitutions limit the power of governments even though governments are elected?
questions.answer: A government with unlimited power could misuse it or harm minorities and individuals, even if a majority elected it. A constitution sets limits so that rights are protected and power is shared among institutions.
keyPoints: Elected governments can still misuse power
Rights of individuals and minorities need protection
questions.explanation: Constitutional limits protect citizens from arbitrary rule.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: For how many years are members of the Lok Sabha normally elected?
questions.explanation: The Lok Sabha has a normal term of five years unless it is dissolved earlier.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Who is the head of the state in India?
questions.explanation: The President is the formal head of the state, while the Prime Minister heads the government.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Which House of Parliament is directly elected by the people?
questions.explanation: Members of the Lok Sabha are chosen by voters in constituencies.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: What is a by-election?
options: An election held to fill a seat that falls vacant between general elections
An election held every five years
An election for the President only
questions.explanation: A seat can fall vacant due to resignation or death, and a by-election fills it.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Why are some constituencies reserved for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes?
options: To keep them away from voting
To reduce the number of seats
To ensure that weaker sections get fair representation in the legislature
questions.explanation: Reservation was meant to ensure that these groups are represented in law-making bodies.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: What is the Council of Ministers?
questions.answer: The Council of Ministers is the Prime Minister together with all the ministers. It runs the government and is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha.
questions.explanation: The ministers are answerable to the elected House.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Why are political parties needed in a representative democracy?
questions.answer: Parties put up candidates in elections, offer policies to voters and organise the government when they win. Parties that lose act as the opposition and question the government.
questions.explanation: Parties connect voters to government and give them a choice.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Which Fundamental Right lets a person follow and practise any religion?
questions.explanation: This right guarantees freedom of conscience and the right to practise and propagate religion.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Which of these is guaranteed under the Right to Freedom?
questions.explanation: The Right to Freedom includes freedom of speech, to assemble peacefully and to form associations.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Which statement about the National Human Rights Commission is correct?
options: It can send offenders to jail
It can inquire into violations of human rights and make recommendations, but it cannot punish
questions.explanation: The Commission has the power to inquire and recommend, but action is taken by the government and courts.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: What does equality before the law mean?
options: All people have the same income
Everyone, including officials, is subject to the same laws
Laws apply only to the poor
questions.explanation: No person is above the law, whatever their position.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: A restaurant refuses to serve a person because of their caste. Which right is violated?
questions.explanation: The Right to Equality prohibits discrimination in access to public places on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Why is the Right to Constitutional Remedies considered so important?
options: It lets citizens go to court to enforce all their other Fundamental Rights
It protects only the property of the rich
questions.explanation: Without a way to enforce them in court, other rights would remain only promises.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: List any three freedoms included in the Right to Freedom.
questions.answer: The Right to Freedom includes freedom of speech and expression, freedom to assemble peacefully, freedom to form associations, freedom to move freely across the country, and freedom to practise any profession.
questions.explanation: These freedoms are subject to reasonable restrictions.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: How does the right to information help a democracy?
questions.answer: The right to information lets citizens ask government offices for records and details of their work. It makes government more open and accountable and helps people detect and prevent wrongdoing.
keyPoints: Citizens can seek information from government
questions.explanation: The Right to Information Act of 2005 gives this power to citizens.

questions.subject: social
questions.topic: Village Economy and People as Resource
questions.q: What is the main source of employment in most Indian villages?
questions.explanation: Most villagers depend on farming and related activities for work.

questions.subject: social
questions.topic: Village Economy and People as Resource
questions.q: A crop sown in winter and harvested in spring, such as wheat, is called a
questions.explanation: Rabi crops are sown in winter and harvested in the spring, while kharif crops are grown in the rainy season.

questions.subject: social
questions.topic: Village Economy and People as Resource
questions.q: Raw materials and money in hand that a farmer needs during production are called
questions.explanation: Working capital is used up in production, unlike tools and machines, which are fixed capital.

questions.subject: social
questions.topic: Village Economy and People as Resource
questions.q: What is the term for a situation in which more people are working on a farm than are needed, so removing some does not reduce output?
questions.explanation: In disguised unemployment people look busy but add nothing extra to production.

questions.subject: social
questions.topic: Village Economy and People as Resource
questions.q: Why do landless farm labourers often earn less than the minimum wages?
options: Many workers compete for few jobs, so they accept low wages
The government pays them more than the minimum
questions.explanation: Lack of other jobs weakens their bargaining power.

questions.subject: social
questions.topic: Village Economy and People as Resource
questions.q: What are non-farm activities? Give two examples.
questions.answer: Non-farm activities are jobs and businesses that are not farming, such as dairy, small-scale manufacturing, shopkeeping and transport.
keyPoints: Examples such as dairy, shops, transport, small manufacturing
questions.explanation: Villages need more non-farm work to raise incomes.

questions.subject: social
questions.topic: Village Economy and People as Resource
questions.q: How can the heavy use of chemical fertilisers and tubewells harm farmland in the long run?
questions.answer: Chemical fertilisers can reduce the natural fertility of soil and pollute water, and over-use of tubewells can lower the water table. Together they can reduce the land's ability to produce in future.
questions.explanation: Short-term gains in output can damage long-term resources.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: What is the condition of not having enough food to eat called?
questions.explanation: Hunger is an indicator of food insecurity and poverty.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: What is a buffer stock?
options: Grain bought by the government and stored to use during shortages
questions.explanation: The Food Corporation of India buys grain in surplus areas and keeps it as a reserve.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Which scheme provides highly subsidised grain to the poorest of the poor families?
questions.explanation: The Antyodaya Anna Yojana was launched in 2000 for the poorest families.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Which of the following is an indicator of poverty besides low income?
questions.explanation: Poor nutrition, lack of education and lack of health care are signs of poverty.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Why does the government announce a minimum support price before the sowing season?
options: To stop farmers from growing crops
To assure farmers of a fair price and encourage them to grow food grains
questions.explanation: A known price reduces the risk for farmers and supports grain production.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Distinguish between chronic hunger and seasonal hunger.
questions.answer: Chronic hunger is a long-term condition in which people consistently eat too little or poor-quality food because of low incomes. Seasonal hunger arises at certain times of the year, for example before harvest or when farm work is scarce.
keyPoints: Seasonal: linked to times of the year or work availability
questions.explanation: The two kinds of hunger have different causes.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: What do we mean by vulnerability to poverty?
questions.answer: Vulnerability describes the greater chance that some groups or families will become or stay poor when bad times come, such as a drought or illness or loss of a job. Landless labourers and poor households face this risk more.
keyPoints: Greater chance of becoming or staying poor
Caused by shocks such as illness or job loss
Affects poor and landless households more
questions.explanation: Vulnerable groups have little to fall back on.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Which leader dominated the Jacobin government during the Reign of Terror of 1793-94?
questions.explanation: Robespierre headed the Jacobin government that carried out the Terror before he was himself overthrown and executed.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Which device, named after a doctor who proposed it, became a symbol of the Reign of Terror?
questions.explanation: The guillotine was meant to give a quick and equal method of execution and was widely used in 1793-94.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: What name was given to the ordinary working people of Paris who did not wear the fashionable knee-length breeches of the nobles?
questions.explanation: Sans-culottes literally means without knee breeches and referred to radical Parisian workers, shopkeepers and artisans.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Why is the period of Jacobin rule from 1793 to 1794 called the Reign of Terror?
options: Those considered enemies of the republic were arrested, tried and often guillotined
Louis XVI ruled with great cruelty
questions.explanation: Under Robespierre, many people were executed on the charge of being enemies of the republic.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Why did many French people accept Napoleon's rise to power in 1799?
options: They disliked all kinds of order
The unstable Directory had lost trust, and Napoleon promised order and stability
He promised to restore the feudal system
questions.explanation: After years of upheaval and an unpopular, unstable government, many wanted a strong ruler.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: What was the National Convention?
questions.answer: The National Convention was the elected assembly of France after 1792, chosen by all men aged twenty-one and above. It abolished the monarchy and declared France a republic.
keyPoints: Elected by all men aged 21 and above
Abolished monarchy and declared a republic
questions.explanation: It marked a wider franchise than the Constitution of 1791.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Describe two measures taken by the Jacobin government to help the poorer sections of society.
questions.answer: The Jacobins fixed maximum prices for essential items such as bread and meat and rationed supplies. They also made everyone use the title citizen and eat the same kind of bread, to promote equality.
keyPoints: Equality symbols such as the title citizen
questions.explanation: These steps responded to the demands of the sans-culottes.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Who organised the Red Army during the Russian Civil War?
questions.explanation: Trotsky built and led the Red Army that fought the opponents of the Bolsheviks.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: What were the soviets in Russia in 1917?
options: Councils of workers, soldiers and peasants
questions.explanation: Soviets were elected councils that became centres of revolutionary power.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: What did Lenin's April Theses of 1917 demand?
options: An end to the war, land for peasants and nationalisation of banks
questions.explanation: The Theses called for peace, transfer of land to peasants and state control of banks.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: In Russia, who were the kulaks?
questions.explanation: The kulaks were better-off peasants who were targeted during Stalin's collectivisation.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Why did the Provisional Government lose support in 1917?
options: It gave all land to peasants at once
It was too small to be noticed
It continued the war and delayed land reform, failing to give people peace and land
questions.explanation: Its failure to meet the demands for peace and land helped the Bolsheviks.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: What was collectivisation in the Soviet Union?
questions.answer: Collectivisation was a policy begun around 1929 under Stalin in which peasants were made to pool their land and tools into large state-controlled collective farms. It was meant to increase grain output but caused hardship and food shortages.
keyPoints: Peasants forced to join collective farms
questions.explanation: The policy changed how land was owned and farmed.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Describe two ways in which the Russian Revolution influenced the world.
questions.answer: It inspired socialist and communist movements in many countries and encouraged workers to demand rights. It also made many leaders in colonised countries interested in ideas of equality and freedom, and it created a socialist state as a rival to capitalist powers.
keyPoints: Created a socialist state as a world power
questions.explanation: The revolution became a major reference point in twentieth-century politics.

questions.subject: social
questions.topic: Nazism and the Rise of Hitler
questions.q: What was the full name of Hitler's party?
questions.explanation: Nazi is short for National Socialist.

questions.subject: social
questions.topic: Nazism and the Rise of Hitler
questions.q: In which year did the Second World War end in Europe with Germany's defeat?
questions.explanation: Germany surrendered in May 1945.

questions.subject: social
questions.topic: Nazism and the Rise of Hitler
questions.q: What was the Gestapo?
options: The secret state police of Nazi Germany
questions.explanation: The Gestapo arrested and terrorised opponents of the regime.

questions.subject: social
questions.topic: Nazism and the Rise of Hitler
questions.q: Which laws of 1935 stripped German Jews of their citizenship and rights?
questions.explanation: The Nuremberg Laws defined Jews as a separate group and took away their rights.

questions.subject: social
questions.topic: Nazism and the Rise of Hitler
questions.q: Why did the hyperinflation of 1923 hurt the German middle class so badly?
options: They had no money at all
Their savings and fixed incomes lost value as prices soared
questions.explanation: Savings became almost worthless, and this fed anger against the Weimar government.

questions.subject: social
questions.topic: Nazism and the Rise of Hitler
questions.q: Why were the Nuremberg Trials held in 1945-46?
options: To try leading Nazi officials for war crimes and crimes against humanity
To elect a new German government
To sign a peace treaty with Japan
questions.explanation: The trials were set up by the Allies to hold top Nazi leaders responsible for their actions.

questions.subject: social
questions.topic: Nazism and the Rise of Hitler
questions.q: Name two weaknesses of the Weimar Republic.
questions.answer: Proportional representation often produced unstable coalition governments, and Article 48 allowed the President to rule by emergency decree, which weakened democratic habits. The republic was also burdened by the Treaty of Versailles.
questions.explanation: These weaknesses made it easier for extremists to rise.

questions.subject: social
questions.topic: Nazism and the Rise of Hitler
questions.q: Why did many Germans support or accept Hitler in the early 1930s?
questions.answer: Hitler promised jobs, economic recovery and national pride at a time of unemployment and humiliation. Effective propaganda, fear of communism and the lack of trust in the Weimar leaders also helped him.
questions.explanation: Economic distress and propaganda together increased his support.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Most of southern India lies on which plateau?
questions.explanation: The Deccan Plateau is the large triangular plateau of the peninsula.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: What is another name for the Himadri range?
questions.explanation: Himadri is the northernmost and highest range of the Himalayas.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Chilika Lake, a large coastal lagoon, is located on the coast of which state?
questions.explanation: Chilika Lake lies on the Odisha coast beside the Bay of Bengal.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: The Purvanchal hills lie in which part of India?
questions.explanation: The Purvanchal hills, including the Patkai and Mizo hills, lie along the eastern border in the north-east.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Why is the Himalayan region more prone to earthquakes than the Peninsular Plateau?
options: The Himalayas are young mountains where the earth's plates are still pushing against each other
The Plateau is covered by water
The Himalayas are made of sand
There are no plates in India
questions.explanation: The ongoing collision of plates keeps the Himalayan region geologically active.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Which statement correctly compares the Western and Eastern Ghats?
options: Eastern Ghats are higher and continuous
Western Ghats are higher and continuous, while Eastern Ghats are lower and broken by rivers
They are not connected to the peninsula
questions.explanation: The Western Ghats are higher and more continuous, while the Eastern Ghats are discontinuous and cut by rivers.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Describe two features of the Indian desert.
questions.answer: The Thar Desert is a dry, sandy plain west of the Aravali hills with sand dunes and very low rainfall. It has scanty vegetation, and the Luni is its only large river.
questions.explanation: Water is scarce, and life depends on special adaptation.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Explain how India's different physical features are useful to its economy.
questions.answer: The plains support agriculture and large populations, mountains provide forests, minerals and tourist places, and rivers give water and hydroelectric power. The plateau is rich in minerals and the coasts have ports.
questions.explanation: Each landform supports different economic activities.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Into which water body does the Ganga finally flow?
questions.explanation: The Ganga reaches the Bay of Bengal, forming a large delta with the Brahmaputra.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Which of these is a tributary of the Ganga?
questions.explanation: The Gandak, Ghaghara, Kosi and Son are among the Ganga's tributaries.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Jog Falls, one of the highest waterfalls in India, is on which river?
questions.explanation: The Sharavati river plunges down the Jog Falls in Karnataka.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Which river is a tributary of the Indus?
questions.explanation: The Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas and Sutlej are tributaries of the Indus system.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: What do the Narmada and Tapi form at their mouths?
questions.explanation: These west-flowing rivers enter the Arabian Sea through estuaries.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Name any three tributaries of the Ganga.
questions.answer: Important tributaries of the Ganga include the Yamuna, Ghaghara, Gandak, Kosi and Son.
questions.explanation: These tributaries join the Ganga on its journey across the northern plains.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Why do Himalayan rivers build large plains while peninsular rivers build fewer?
questions.answer: Himalayan rivers flow down steep slopes and carry large amounts of eroded material, which they spread across the gentle plains. Peninsular rivers flow over old, hard rocks with less erosion and smaller loads of silt.
keyPoints: Himalayan rivers erode steep young mountains
Large load of silt deposited on plains
questions.explanation: The amount of sediment depends on the slope and rock type.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Which is the hottest season in most parts of India?
questions.explanation: Temperatures rise sharply in the hot weather season, especially in the north.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: What is the sudden arrival of the monsoon rain, with thunder and lightning, usually called?
questions.explanation: The monsoon arrives with a sudden burst of rain after the hot summer.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: What mainly causes the monsoon winds to reverse their direction between summer and winter?
options: The unequal heating of land and sea
questions.explanation: The land heats and cools faster than the sea, changing the pressure pattern and wind direction.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Which region of India receives the lowest rainfall?
questions.explanation: Western Rajasthan is far from the sea and receives very little rain.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Why does a weak monsoon affect India's economy so strongly?
options: Roads cannot be built in dry weather
Rain is not used in agriculture
Agriculture depends heavily on rain, so poor rainfall lowers output, incomes and raises food prices
questions.explanation: A large share of people depend on farming, which relies on the monsoon.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Why does Mumbai get heavy rain in the south-west monsoon while Chennai remains comparatively dry in those months?
options: Mumbai lies on the windward side of the Western Ghats, while Chennai lies in their rain shadow
Mumbai is at a higher altitude
questions.explanation: The Western Ghats force moist winds to rain on the western side, leaving Tamil Nadu on the leeward side.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Name four factors that affect the climate of India.
questions.answer: The climate of India is affected by latitude, altitude, pressure and wind systems, distance from the sea, ocean currents and relief features.
questions.explanation: A combination of these factors gives India its varied climate.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Why is the cold weather season generally cooler in north India than in south India?
questions.answer: North India lies farther from the equator, so the sun's rays are less direct. It is also far from the moderating influence of the sea and is open to cold winds from the north, while the south is nearer the equator and the sea.
questions.explanation: Latitude and distance from the sea explain the difference.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Which animal is found in the Rann of Kachchh?
questions.explanation: The Indian wild ass is found in the Rann of Kachchh in Gujarat.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Which of these is a national park of India?
questions.explanation: Jim Corbett National Park in Uttarakhand was the first national park of India.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Which forest type is also known as the monsoon forest?
questions.explanation: The tropical deciduous forests respond to the seasonal rhythm of the monsoon.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: What is the main feature of deciduous trees?
options: They shed their leaves in the dry season to conserve water
questions.explanation: Shedding leaves reduces water loss during the dry months.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Why does natural vegetation on a tall Himalayan slope change as we climb higher?
options: Soil is the same at every height
Temperature falls with altitude, so vegetation changes from tropical to temperate to alpine
Rainfall is equal at all levels
questions.explanation: Vegetation follows the change in temperature and moisture with height.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Name any four types of natural vegetation found in India.
questions.answer: The types of vegetation include tropical evergreen forests, tropical deciduous forests, tropical thorn forests and scrub, montane forests, and mangrove forests.
questions.explanation: The kind of vegetation depends on rainfall, temperature and soil.

questions.subject: social
questions.q: Give three reasons why forests should be conserved.
questions.answer: Forests give timber, fuel and other products to people and provide homes to wildlife. They also protect soil from erosion, help rainfall and keep the air clean by absorbing carbon dioxide.
